item.text: {"text":"Recent work supports separating sequence sensitivity from popularity effects. “Lost in Sequence” (KDD 2025) finds existing LLM recommenders often fail to capture sequential information during training and inference, motivating order-shuffling diagnostics ([paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.13909)). “Robust Training of Sequential Recommender Systems with Missing Input Data” reports strong dependence on recent interactions: removing SASRec’s last input item displaced the previously top-ranked item by over 25 positions on average in its MovieLens-1M experiment; earlier-item removal had smaller effects ([paper](https://assets.amazon.science/ea/6b/d2f305e64d1394abe7839be6e976/robust-training-of-sequential-recommender-systems-with-missing-input-data.pdf)). A 2024 negative-sampling study finds aggregate accuracy conceals head/mid/tail differences; random sampling favors head items, while popularity-based sampling can improve balance at an accuracy cost ([paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17276)).\n\nSuggested diagnostic synthesis, rather than an established recipe from these papers: freeze the trained model and compare deployed transition residuals with zero correction, popularity-only correction, and shuffled transitions preserving source and destination counts. Shuffle transition destinations across observed edges to retain these marginals while disrupting pair identity; repeat with several seeds. Separately perturb recent versus older history using matched numbers of edits, preserving sequence length and item multiplicities for permutation controls. On identical validation users and candidates, report paired target-rank changes and HR@10 differences, stratified by training-only transition support, history length, and target popularity; summarize all four categories with the required macro-average. Gains surviving shuffled transitions suggest a marginal-frequency mechanism; gains specific to intact transitions support useful pair information. These interventions diagnose model behavior, not causal user preferences or unobserved conformity."}
